problems.title: Induction for divisibility by nineteen
problems.question: Prove that $F_n=5\cdot2^{3n-2}+3^{3n-1}$ is divisible by 19 for every positive integer n.
problems.idea: Express the next case as a multiple of the current case plus an obvious multiple of 19.
formulas: Mathematical induction: verify n=1, then prove the implication n→n+1.
steps: Base case: F₁=5·2+3²=19.
Assume 19 divides Fₙ. In Fₙ₊₁ the first term is 8 times the previous first term and the second is 27 times the previous second term.
Both summands are divisible by 19, so the next case holds. Induction proves every positive n.

problems.title: Two geometric progressions fit the same pair sums
problems.question: A geometric progression has first plus fourth term 35 and second plus third term 30. Find the sum of its first five terms.
problems.idea: Solve for the ratio, keeping both reciprocal possibilities.
steps: The second sum is 30, so q≠0,-1. Dividing the sums gives q+1/q-1=35/30=7/6.
For q=3/2, u=30/[q(1+q)]=8; the five terms are 8,12,18,27,81/2, summing to 211/2.
For q=2/3, u=27; the five terms are 27,18,12,8,16/3, summing to 211/3.
problems.note: Both ratios satisfy all the stated conditions. A unique sum requires a condition such as an increasing progression.

problems.title: A reordered arithmetic progression becomes geometric
problems.question: The second, first and third terms of an arithmetic progression, in that order, form a geometric progression. Find its ratio.
problems.idea: Write the arithmetic terms as a,a+d,a+2d.
formulas: Three consecutive geometric terms satisfy middle²=first·third.
steps: The reordered terms give a²=(a+d)(a+2d), hence d(3a+2d)=0.
If the progression is nonconstant, d=-3a/2; the reordered nonzero terms are -a/2,a,-2a, with common ratio -2.
If d=0 and a≠0, the reordered constant progression has ratio 1.
If all terms are zero, the ratio is not uniquely determined.
problems.answer: -2 for the nonconstant case; 1 for a nonzero constant progression.
problems.note: The problem does not exclude a constant arithmetic progression, so the stated data permit both ordinary ratios.

problems.title: Induction for a telescoping product
problems.question: Prove $\prod_{k=2}^{n+1}(1-1/k^2)=(n+2)/(2n+2)$ for n≥1.
problems.idea: Multiply the induction formula by the single new factor.
steps: At n=1 the product is 1-1/4=3/4, matching (1+2)/(2+2).
Assume the formula at n. The next product is [(n+2)/(2n+2)]·[1-1/(n+2)²].
Replace the final factor by (n+1)(n+3)/(n+2)² and cancel to get (n+3)/[2(n+2)].
This is exactly the claimed expression with n replaced by n+1.
problems.answer: The identity holds for every positive integer n.

problems.title: An infinite sum of shrinking hexagon perimeters
problems.question: A regular hexagon has side 6 cm. Repeatedly join side midpoints to form new regular hexagons. Find the sum of all their perimeters, including the original.
problems.idea: Each midpoint hexagon has a fixed similarity ratio.
formulas: The ratio is cos30°=√3/2; an infinite geometric series has sum P/(1-q) for |q|<1.
steps: The original perimeter is 6·6=36.
Joining adjacent midpoints multiplies every length by √3/2.
Rationalizing gives 72(2+√3).

problems.title: Root relations plus a geometric progression
problems.question: The roots x₁,x₂ of x²-6px-2q=0 occur in the geometric progression p,x₁,x₂,q. Find the roots.
problems.idea: Use a common ratio t and Vieta’s formulas.
steps: In the nonzero case, write x₁=pt,x₂=pt²,q=pt³. The product relation gives p²t³=-2pt³, so p=-2.
The sum relation gives t+t²=6, so t=2 or -3.
For t=2, the ordered roots are (-4,-8). For t=-3, they are (6,-18).
If a zero progression is allowed, p=q=x₁=x₂=0 also satisfies the equations; it has a repeated zero root.
problems.answer: (-4,-8) or (6,-18); additionally (0,0) if the all-zero degenerate progression is allowed.
problems.note: A nonzero geometric progression yields the first two possibilities. Distinct roots or the standard nonzero-term convention excludes the degenerate zero case.

problems.title: Vector to an angle-bisector foot
problems.question: In ABC, AD is the internal bisector. AB=a, AC=b as vectors, with |a|:|b|=2:3. Find AD.
problems.idea: Use the angle-bisector ratio on BC and the section formula.
formulas: BD:DC=AB:AC; a division point with ratio m:n has vector (nB+mC)/(m+n).
steps: The bisector theorem gives BD:DC=2:3.
With A as origin, B=a and C=b.
Therefore D=(3a+2b)/5, which is also vector AD.

problems.title: A length condition forces a zero dot product
problems.question: M,N,K,P lie on AB,BC,CD,AD of square ABCD, with NC+CK=BM+PD. Find MK·NP.
problems.idea: Choose coordinates and translate the length condition into a simple equality.
steps: The given lengths give (s-n)+(s-k)=(s-m)+(s-p), hence m+p=n+k.
MK=(k-m,s) and NP=(-s,p-n).
Their dot product is s(m+p-n-k)=0.
problems.answer: 0; the two vectors are perpendicular when nonzero.

problems.title: Cosine at the crossing of two rectangle segments
problems.question: In rectangle ABCD, AB=6,AD=8. M lies on BC with BM:MC=3:1, and N on CD with CN:ND=2:1. AM and BN meet at K. Find cosAKB.
problems.idea: Find the crossing in coordinates and use the two requested ray vectors.
steps: AM is y=x; BN is y=-2x+12. Thus K=(4,4).
KA=(-4,-4),KB=(2,-4). Their dot product is 8 and their lengths are 4√2,2√5.
Hence cosAKB=8/(8√10)=1/√10.

problems.title: Points that make all three triangle angles acute
problems.question: O=(0,0),N=(9,0), and X lies on y=4. Find all X for which OXN is acute.
problems.idea: At each vertex, the dot product of the two outward side vectors must be positive.
formulas: An angle is acute iff its two side vectors have positive dot product.
steps: Write X=(t,4). At O the condition is 9t>0, giving t>0. At N it is 9(9-t)>0, giving t<9.
At X, the vectors (-t,-4),(9-t,-4) have dot product t²-9t+16.
Its zeros are (9±√17)/2, and it is positive outside those zeros.
Intersect with 0<t<9 to get the two stated intervals.
